The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Helios Towers (HTWS-GB): EBITDA growth of about 13% is close to settled through FY2027, which makes the shares dependable delivery at a reasonable price, and the first half of 2027 is when the share price is most likely to part from the fundamentals

Written 24 November 2026 for Richard. Share price 237p on 17 November 2026 (about USD 3.12), the price used in the Financial Analyst's model. Money is in USD millions unless stated. Definitions, sources and the two bases of EPS are set out in the reading notes at the end.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in three sentences. Helios leases tower space and power to mobile operators in nine African and Middle Eastern markets under long, inflation-indexed, non-cancellable contracts, and it is the leading independent tower owner in seven of those markets. Operators added tenancies at a record pace in 2026, and because a tenancy added in one year earns its first full year of revenue in the next, EBITDA growth of about 13% is close to settled for both FY2026 and FY2027. The market already knows this, so the probability of upgrades is not unusually skewed to the positive today: the shares offer dependable delivery at a reasonable price, and the first half of 2027 is when the share price is most likely to part from the fundamentals.

The six insights that matter most

  1. The business outcome is narrow, but the equity outcome is wide. FY2027 EBITDA should land within about 3% of the forecast four times in five. Reported EPS for the same year has a range of about minus 40% to plus 12%, because tax, currency and the share count are not guided. The case is therefore best judged on EBITDA, recurring free cash flow per share and leverage.
  2. Whether the skew is positive depends on the yardstick. Against the company's own guidance, raises are close to certain. Against consensus there is no gap, because brokers have learnt the pattern of raises and already forecast the level to which guidance will be raised.
  3. The optics and the fundamentals part company in the first half of 2027. In that half-year tenancy additions will fall about 40% year on year, FY2027 guidance will probably open on 18 March with a midpoint below consensus, reported FY2026 EPS will probably miss consensus, and a convertible bond may add shares. In the same half-year EBITDA growth peaks at about 15%. This mismatch between optics and fundamentals is the main near-term hazard in the case and, because the EBITDA is largely installed already, also its main source of opportunity.
  4. The composition of growth has changed more than its level. High-return colocations have fallen back to their 2025 pace, and capital-heavy new towers have taken their place. The volume of additions stays high, but each tenancy now costs more capital, and the company's 2030 target for the tenancy ratio is at risk.
  5. The dependable return is earnings growth. At an unchanged multiple, the model's earnings and dividends give a total return of about 26% to 31 December 2027, roughly 17% to 19% a year. The model's return of record, +256.1%, rests on a guideline fair multiple of 42.33x that I think overstates what investors will pay (#11). My own fair multiple of about 20x adds about 12%.
  6. The risks that could break the case sit in the DRC. The DRC is Helios's largest market and the place where the installed base could be reopened, either through the terms of contract renewals or through a law requiring 30% local ownership of telecom operators by July 2027. Nobody has yet shown whether that law applies to tower companies or exempts them.

Implications for Richard. The operating case can be owned with confidence through FY2027. A weak share price in the first half of 2027, caused by optics while EBITDA growth peaks, would be an opportunity rather than a warning. Four dates settle most of the uncertainty: late January 2027 (Airtel Africa's capex), 18 March 2027 (Helios's results, FY2027 guidance, tax, currency and the convertible), May 2027 (Airtel's capex guidance for its year to March 2028) and November 2027 (the first view of Helios's FY2028 volume). One question deserves research now: whether the DRC ownership law reaches tower companies.

#1 Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Bottom lineThe operating environment is a strong tailwind for EBITDA through FY2027 and a moderate headwind for the equity that is not improving. The DRC ownership law is the one headwind that nobody has priced.

Evidence: demand is structural and deep. African mobile operators are in a capex surge because data demand is outgrowing their networks, and Helios's order book reflects that surge.

75% vs 15%
Share of data carried on mobile networks, Africa against Europe
35% / 45%
Mobile population coverage in the DRC and Tanzania
+56%
Airtel Africa's data traffic growth in a year
121 → 389
Airtel Africa's capex, June 2025 quarter against June 2026 quarter

Helios's tenancy additions rose from 2,538 in FY2025 to about 4,000 guided for FY2026, and management has guided more than 3,000 for FY2027 from customer orders already in hand.

Two facts qualify the tailwind.

First, the operators' capex surge is front-loaded. Airtel Africa kept its full-year capex guidance at 1.1 USDbn after spending 657 in its first half, which implies about a third less capex per quarter in its second half. Helios's quarterly additions in 2026 followed the same path: 1,406, 1,105 and 924, with about 565 implied for Q4.

Second, the mix of Helios's additions has turned towards new towers. New towers were 45% of Q3 2026 additions (418 of 924), against 16.6% in FY2025 and a long-run company guide of 25%. Colocations, at about 506 in Q3, are back at their 2025 quarterly pace.

The headwinds act on the equity, not on EBITDA.

  • Sovereign and currency risk. Moody's cut Senegal's rating to Ca on 4 November 2026. The DRC bans physical foreign-currency cash from 9 April 2027, but Helios bills in dollars and collects electronically, so the ban's direct effect on Helios should be small. About 32% of Helios's revenue is billed in local currencies.
  • Interest rates. A US ten-year yield near 5% weighs on towers as a sector, although Helios's share price has decoupled from the sector (#8).
  • Customers becoming competitors. Rival tower companies are retreating: American Tower favours developed markets, and MTN is buying IHS. The new competitor is the customer. Vodacom and Orange formed Esengo Towers to build 1,000 rural towers in the DRC, Indus Towers is following Airtel into Africa, and Vodacom and Airtel have agreed to share networks in Tanzania and the DRC.
  • Two risks that broker research has not yet connected to Helios. The first is the DRC's local-ownership law (#9). The second is a 40% fall in African smartphone shipments in Q3 2026 (Omdia data), which may be a lead indicator for operators' capacity orders.

Inference. The level of demand for new tenancies is secure through FY2027, but the quality of that demand has changed. Growth has shifted from densifying existing towers, which earns very high returns, to building coverage with new towers, which earns returns near the cost of capital. Visibility on orders ends at the end of 2027, and three forces then point the same way: the front-loading of operators' capex, network sharing and customer-owned towers. These three forces threaten new builds and future colocations, but they leave the installed tenancies untouched.

So what. The tailwinds belong in the operating lines of the forecasts, and the headwinds belong in the tax, currency and finance lines and in the multiple. Helios's volume of additions holds for a year longer than the operators' capex data alone would suggest, but at a higher capital cost per tenancy.

Counter-case. The operators' capex cycle could end faster than the base case assumes: Airtel could pause after its front-loaded year, weak handset sales could slow data growth, and Esengo could take the rural builds. Helios's additions would then fall to about 1,500 a year from FY2028, which is Morgan Stanley's bear case.

What would change my view
  • Positive: Airtel's capex guidance for its year to March 2028, due in May 2027. Deutsche Bank expects 1.0 USDbn after 1.1 USDbn; a figure clearly above 1.0 USDbn would argue for a longer cycle.
  • Negative: Indus Towers entering one of Helios's markets, or a ruling that the DRC ownership law covers towers.
Where I agree with the market

The brokers and I agree on the strength of demand.

Where I differ

I treat the shift to new towers as a real rise in capital intensity, where the brokers treat it as future capacity for colocations. I also carry two risks that brokers have not connected to Helios.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Structural African data demand (75% of data on mobile, 35-45% coverage in the DRC and Tanzania, Airtel traffic +56%) drove a record capex surge that holds tenancy additions near 3,100 in FY2027 from orders in hand, so the tailwind reaches the whole business with high visibility for about a year; it is front-loaded (Airtel's H2 run-rate a third lower), shifting to capital-heavy coverage builds, and directly threatened after 2027 by network sharing and customer-owned towers (Esengo, Indus following Airtel). The 70th-percentile consensus sales growth fits; I agree with the group's 68 and place it just below Spie, which has a longer horizon, and above Odfjell's two-year contracted cycle because the demand is structural.

#2 Internal corporate change

Bottom lineHelios's corporate change is strong, funded and well executed along one axis, capital allocation. Its main test is whether management stays disciplined with surplus cash from 2028.

Evidence. At the end of 2022 Helios stopped acquiring towers and turned to filling the towers it owns and returning cash to shareholders. It has bought nothing since, and the results of that turn showed fully in 2026.

  • Dividend. Helios declared its first dividend, about 25 for FY2026, and guided it to grow by more than 10% a year.
  • Balance sheet. A 500 issue of 6.75% notes due 2031 lowered the blended cost of debt, and all three rating agencies upgraded Helios's credit (Moody's to Ba3).
  • Targets. The IMPACT 2030 plan commits to more than 42,000 tenancies, a tenancy ratio above 2.5x, EBITDA growth above 9% a year, more than 1.3 USDbn of cumulative recurring free cash flow and at least 400 of distributions.
  • Execution. Besides the faster tower builds, Helios now delivers a colocation within a day or two.

The negatives are smaller, but real.

  • Discretionary capex was 172.8 in the first nine months of 2026, against 72.0 a year earlier.
  • A 150 commitment to Senegal, whose towers average 1.24 tenants and whose sovereign is near default, sits oddly with the company's stated return threshold of 20% to 35%.
  • The chief executive sold 24% of his shares in March 2026, the maximum levels of executive pay were raised, and the board is only 50% independent.
  • The founding shareholders have sold down. Their exit removed an overhang on the shares and, at the same time, removed a check on management.

Inference. Helios is in a harvest phase. The harvest is predictable, funded from recurring free cash flow and run by an unchanged team. It is also narrow: there is no pricing lever, no cost programme and no change to the group's perimeter. The internal changes therefore add certainty to cash and distributions, but they add no growth beyond what operators' demand supplies.

So what. Internal change underwrites the cash-return part of the shareholder return. It does little for EPS, because interest at Helios's holding companies earns no tax relief, which makes buying back shares and repaying debt close to equivalent for EPS (#5).

Counter-case. The last time Helios had room on its balance sheet, in 2020 to 2022, it spent that room on acquisitions that initially earned about 6%. IMPACT 2030 carries a 400 line of "flexible capital", leverage reaches about 3.0x by the end of 2027, and no large shareholder now sits on the board to restrain a repeat.

What would change my view
  • Negative: an acquisition outside the nine existing markets, or a buyback slowed to fund capex.
  • Positive: a successor buyback around December 2027, which I put at about 70% likely.

Against the market. Brokers present the step-up in distributions as the next catalyst. I agree on the direction but not on the novelty: brokers already publish distribution capacity of two to four times the company's floor, so a larger programme would confirm their numbers rather than raise them.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. A funded, well-executed capital-allocation harvest since 2022 (no acquisitions, leverage 5.1x to 3.4x, three credit upgrades, cost of debt down 0.4 points, buyback raised to 175, a first dividend, build time cut from 167 to 102 days) is real and in the numbers, but it adds certainty to cash rather than growth: no pricing, cost or perimeter lever, and the memo shows buybacks add little EPS at this price. Discretionary capex more than doubling, a 150 Senegal commitment against the stated return gate, chief executive selling and a 50%-independent board trim it; with the group's 61, this is complete self-help that improves a mature model, in the low 60s per the levels.

#3 Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Bottom lineThe industry structure, Helios's moat and its management are favourable and proven. The weak points are customer concentration and an earnings base that is clean only down to EBITDA.

Evidence

  • Industry structure. Helios owns 75% of the independent towers in the DRC and 60% of all marketable towers in Tanzania, and its rivals put returns before volume. A new entrant needs 100,000 to 150,000 USD per tower, permits, and the ability to keep sites powered where the grid supplies only 8 to 17 hours a day. Helios delivers 99.99% uptime.
  • Contracts. Initial terms are 10 to 15 years with automatic renewals. Renewal is all-or-nothing for the operator, cancellation is capped at about 1% of tenancies a year, and inflation escalators are uncapped. Contracted revenue totals 6.2 USDbn over an average of 6.4 years. Leasing costs an operator about 30% less than owning the tower.
  • Renewals in practice (new evidence). The initial terms on the original DRC portfolios have already expired (Orange's in October 2023 and Airtel's in July 2026), and the contracts have continued. Morgan Stanley reports that the contracts were extended after some network replanning, and Vodacom Tanzania reports that it activated an automatic renewal clause. The terms of the extensions have not been disclosed.
  • Customers. Four operators provide 72% of revenue.
  • Financial profile. Against the European tower companies, Helios grows faster and carries less debt, and its EBITDA margin is lower only because it passes power costs through to customers at no margin (table below). Helios's net earnings are not clean: its reported tax rate was 71% in FY2025, and a 2024 extension of the accounting lives of its towers from 15 to 30 years cut depreciation by 52.8 a year.
  • Management. The chief executive has been at the company for 16 years. Helios has met or beaten every operating guide since 2023, and EBITDA has grown for ten consecutive years, through Ghana's default and conflict in eastern DRC. The blemish on the record is the acquisition wave that the chief executive helped lead before 2022.

Inference. Helios's moat is strong against rival tower companies and against an operator's own cost of building a tower. The moat does not give pricing power, and it does not protect Helios against a customer that decides to build its own towers or to share networks.

On renewals I part from the earlier research work, which treated 2028 to 2029 as a dated, all-or-nothing renewal event. The evidence instead describes renewal by default, with continuous bargaining over energy terms and capex. The company's schedule of contracted revenue falls in 2028 and 2029 only because the schedule assumes that no contract renews.

So what. The installed base of tenancies is close to unassailable through FY2027, and that is what makes the forecasts close to mechanical. Helios's financial profile is above average on growth, leverage and cash, and below average on the level of its margin and on the cleanliness of its net earnings.

Counter-case. Helios's customers have both the motive and the means to push back. Vodacom said on 10 November 2026 that it is renegotiating tower leases as part of its cost programme. A former Helios sales manager says that rates fall 20% to 30% at renewal once the tower has been paid for, and IHS conceded rates to MTN in Nigeria. A price concession could already be hidden inside the undisclosed extensions.

What would change my view
  • A disclosed rate cut at any renewal.
  • The best gauge is contracted revenue for Central and Southern Africa in 2029 and 2030 (395.1 and 363.2 at Q3 2026). A rise beyond what new tenancies explain would show that renewals are being signed.

Against the market. On renewals I agree with the market, which does not treat them as a cliff. I differ in giving more weight to customer-owned towers as an alternative for new builds after 2027.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Qualitative parts are good: leader in seven of nine markets (75% of DRC independent towers), 10-15 year non-cancellable indexed contracts that have renewed by default, 99.99% uptime as an entry barrier, and a management with an unbroken operating record, but the moat protects volume not price, four operators give 72% of revenue and are becoming competitors, the markets are frontier sovereigns, and governance is weak. The financial profile is mixed: the 90th-percentile EBITDA margin and company ROIC of 14.4% with new capital earning about 20% pre-tax against an 11% cost of capital contrast with a 17th-percentile reported ROIC and unclean net earnings (71% tax rate, life extension); coherent with groups of 72/64/50/70, I place it just below Tele2's rational, recurring oligopoly in a safer jurisdiction.

#4 Guidance: conservatism and track record

Bottom lineHelios's guidance is conservative and its record of delivery is among the best in the sector, but the sell-side has already priced in the conservatism, so raises to guidance no longer mean upgrades to consensus.

Evidence. In every year with data, the EBITDA outcome landed at the top of the opening guidance range or up to 2% above it: 370 against 350 to 365 in FY2023, 421 against 405 to 420 in FY2024, and about 535 against 510 to 525 in FY2026. Volume guidance was beaten by far more. The FY2026 additions guide opened at 2,000 to 2,500 and now stands at about 4,000, up 78% on the midpoint, while the EBITDA guide rose only 3%, because tenancies added late in a year earn little revenue in that year.

Below EBITDA there is no guidance, and the brokers' forecasts show it. Consensus EPS for FY2025 fell 53% in the twelve months before the results were published. For FY2026, a year that is now eleven months complete, brokers' EPS forecasts run from 0.054 to 0.130, while their EBITDA forecasts are only 3% apart.

Inference. Helios's guidance is a floor built from customer orders, which is why the company has never had to reverse it. The 3% EBITDA raise and the 78% volume raise of 2026 are the same event seen in two years: the volume raises of 2026 become the EBITDA of 2027. However, the brokers have learnt this pattern, so consensus for FY2027 already sits where guidance will be raised to. The company keeps expectations conservative on the lines it guides and leaves the other lines unanchored.

So what. "Conservative guidance" is true against the company's own delivery but no longer true against the sell-side. I expect FY2027 EBITDA guidance to open on 18 March 2027 at about 585 to 605. That range applies the opening spreads of earlier years to the FY2026 outcome of about 535, and it is consistent with management's statement that FY2027 EBITDA will grow by at least 10%, a floor of about 589. The midpoint of that range would be about 2.5% below consensus, and I expect the FY2027 outcome at about 600 to 615.

Counter-case. Management broke its habit in November by giving a FY2027 volume figure early. With order visibility this good, management could open FY2027 guidance at a range that brackets consensus, which would be a positive surprise. I put the probability of that at 20% to 25%.

What would change my view. An opening range centred on 610 or above, or any guidance on finance costs, tax or the company's own Adjusted EPS, a measure Helios began publishing with its FY2025 results.

Against the market. Brokers describe Helios as a "beat and raise" story. I agree that guidance will be raised, but I expect no beat against consensus.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. EBITDA has landed at or up to 2% above the top of the opening range in every year since 2023, the FY2026 volume guide rose 78%, guidance was raised at three events in 2026 and EBITDA has grown ten years running, so the operating record is near-unbroken and conservative. It is held back because consensus already sits where guidance will be raised to (FY2027 opening midpoint likely 2.5% below consensus), nothing is guided below EBITDA, and FY2025 consensus EPS fell 53% before the print, so the record of raising sell-side EPS estimates is poor; this is the levels' 75 description exactly, consistent with groups of 75 for guidance and 42 for estimates.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage and feedback loops

Bottom lineOperating and financial leverage roughly double EBITDA growth by the time it reaches pre-tax profit. Pricing contributes nothing beyond inflation indexation, and the reinforcing loop from new towers gaining further tenants is the one mechanism still to be proven.

Evidence

  • Operating leverage. Of about 420 of annual cash costs, about 200 is power passed through to customers and about 215 is largely fixed. A new tenancy brings about 27,700 USD of revenue and about 20,000 USD of EBITDA a year. Management's rule of thumb is that 500 tenancies add about 5 of EBITDA in the year they arrive and more than 10 a year after that.
  • Financial leverage. Net financial items are a fixed block of about 185 a year, and more than 90% of the debt is at fixed rates or hedged.
  • Pricing. Inflation escalators add 2% to 3% a year to gross revenue per tenancy, but revenue per tenancy has been flat in dollars after currency and mix effects. There are no real price rises.
  • Costs. Helios has no cost programme and does not need one, because cutting site costs would damage uptime, which is the product customers pay for. The lever is capital: capex falls from 290 in FY2026 to 161 in FY2030.
  • Feedback loops. Each added tenant raises a tower's return and also raises the operator's cost of leaving. New towers of recent vintages gained a second tenant in about 2.5 years. Working against this loop, the more of the density profit Helios keeps, the more reason its customers have to build their own towers or to share networks.

Inference. Helios's revenue growth does lead to outsized profit growth, and the amplification comes from volume spread over fixed costs and fixed interest, with none of it from price.

Two less obvious properties follow from this structure.

  1. Volume and capex are one driver seen twice, and their effects offset. Five hundred fewer tenancy additions cost about 5 of EBITDA in the year and save about 24 of capex. Free cash flow therefore rises when volume disappoints, while EPS falls. An investment case stated on cash per share is better hedged than one stated on EPS.
  2. Buybacks add little to EPS at today's share price. Interest paid by Helios's holding companies earns no tax relief, so debt costs about 7% after tax. The shares' earnings yield on the model's FY2027 EPS is about 6%. Retiring shares and retiring debt are therefore close to equivalent for EPS, and EPS is robust to how cash is returned.

So what. Each 1% change in EBITDA is worth a little over 2% of pre-tax profit, in both directions. The operating half of that gearing has a floor, because revenue on installed tenancies cannot fall; the financial half of the gearing has no such floor.

Counter-case. EBITDA flatters the new towers. A tower's ground lease is booked as depreciation and interest rather than as an EBITDA cost, so the 2026 to 2027 build programme looks better in EBITDA than it will in cash. Rural towers with a single tenant may also fill far more slowly than recent urban towers. Helios's towers in Senegal and Madagascar are still at 1.24 and 1.32 tenants four to five years after purchase, which suggests 0.05 to 0.1 colocations per tower a year, where the company's recent vintages imply 0.4.

What would change my view. Colocations back above 60% of additions by mid-2027 would confirm the reinforcing loop. A tenancy ratio stuck near 2.26x through 2027 would refute it.

Against the market. Brokers take the EBITDA margin to 60% by 2030 on a tenancy ratio above 2.5x. The model reaches a margin of about 59% with a tenancy ratio of only 2.43x, so I expect Helios to miss its tenancy-ratio target while beating its tenancy target.

Score: 73, set by the Rater. Two gears are proven together: about 215 of non-pass-through cash costs are fixed with an incremental EBITDA margin of about 72% per tenancy, and a fixed, over-90%-hedged finance block of about 185 makes each 1% of EBITDA worth about 2% of pre-tax profit (FY2027: revenue +9%, EBITDA +13%, pre-tax +27%), plus a proven colocation density loop (tower returns 12% to 25% to 34%). Pricing is absent beyond indexation (flat revenue per tenancy in dollars), there is no cost-out scope, power pass-through dilutes the gearing and the loop on new rural towers is unproven, so it sits just below the levels' 75 with forecast EPS growth about three times revenue growth.

#6 Forecast financials

Bottom lineThe forecasts offer two more years of double-digit EBITDA growth and four years of mid-to-high-teens EPS growth, with high confidence to FY2027 and moderate confidence after that.

Evidence. The forecasts themselves are in the table in #0. Against the past, the forecasts show slower organic growth at the top and a sharp improvement at the bottom.

FY2019 to FY2025FY2025 to FY2030 (model)
Revenue growth a year14.1%, about half acquired8.0%, all organic
EBITDA growth a yearabout 18%9.6%
EBITDA marginup about 11 pointsup about 4 points
Net incomelosses every year to FY2023156 rising to 272
Free cash flownegative every year to FY2023(56) rising to 244
Share countrisingfalling about 13% from FY2026 to FY2030

Within the next 18 months, revenue growth and EBITDA growth diverge sharply. The cause is fuel: higher fuel prices passed through to customers add about 30 to FY2026 revenue at no margin, and that effect fades in the second half of 2027.

Inference. There is scope for double-digit EBITDA growth for two more years and for mid-to-high-teens EPS growth for four (the model has EPS growth of +24%, +19%, +16% and +17% for FY2027 to FY2030). Revenue, EBITDA and margins grow more slowly than in the past. EPS and free cash flow are the lines that do better than the past, because interest is fixed, capex falls and the share count shrinks. The drivers are concentrated: tenancy volume explains 85% to 90% of the EBITDA increase to FY2028, and the fall in capex explains most of the swing in free cash flow.

So what: three rules for using the forecasts.

  1. Read EBITDA in dollars, not revenue growth or margin. Reported revenue growth will fall by two-thirds within a year, and the EBITDA margin will rise by about three points, with no change in the underlying business.
  2. FY2026 and FY2027 are mostly history already. By September 2026, 3,435 of the year's tenancies were installed. From FY2028 the forecasts depend on tenancies not yet ordered, and they are set at what a precedent delivered after a capex peak (Indus Towers grew EBITDA about 6% a year after India's 5G build).
  3. Part of the per-share growth rests on capital-return policy. The model assumes buybacks of 150, 200 and 225 in FY2028 to FY2030, but only 175 is committed. Because buybacks and debt repayment are close to equivalent for EPS (#5), a smaller programme would change EPS little.

A correction to the model's leverage. The model's net debt of 1,958 at end-2026 looks 100 to 120 too high against the company's own figure of 1,818 at September 2026. The error overstates leverage and leaves EPS unaffected. On the company's basis, leverage falls from about 3.2x at end-2026 to about 2.5x by 2030. The point is an open note to the Financial Analyst.

Counter-case. FY2028 is the year in which the forecast can be wrong in either direction. Morgan Stanley (698) and Deutsche Bank (685) assume that additions stay high and that renewals bring no concession. A sharper pause by operators would put FY2028 EBITDA nearer 640.

What would change my view. The first view of FY2028 volume in November 2027, and the colocation share of additions through 2027.

Against the market. The model is 0.7% below consensus EBITDA for FY2027 and 2.5% below for FY2028, 1% to 3% below consensus on revenue, and above consensus on FY2027 capex (235 against 212). On EPS measured on the same basis, the difference is negligible.

Score: 92, set by the Rater. About 20% sits in the 15-30% A band; the growth is all organic and the EBITDA margin rises to about 59%, above anything in the record, which would place it well inside the band. I hold it near the floor because it is front-loaded (+24% then 16-17%), rests on fixed finance costs gearing slowing EBITDA growth (13% falling to 6%), and part of the per-share growth relies on buybacks not yet committed.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Bottom lineThere is little scope for upgrades to consensus over the next 6 to 12 months. The first event that could reopen that scope is Airtel Africa's capex guidance in May 2027.

Evidence. The research Analysts assessed each event of the next twelve months, and I adopt their probabilities.

One mechanical support for consensus exists. New Street's estimates date from 25 September 2026 and are well below the other brokers' estimates; when New Street refreshes them, the consensus average will rise without any broker changing its mind.

Inference. Helios's guidance will be raised, and consensus will mostly stand still. The narrative has the same shape: every favourable dynamic is already in broker notes, and the items that brokers have not yet discussed would mostly temper enthusiasm. Those items are the fall in additions, capex guidance above consensus, the convertible bond and the DRC ownership law.

So what. Over the next six months the balance of surprise is neutral to slightly negative. Over months 6 to 12, raises bring guidance up to consensus but not above it. A re-rating would need the narrative to move from "volume growth" to "cash per share", and the accounts will start to support that new narrative only once capex falls in FY2028.

Counter-case: five sources of real upgrades.

  1. Operators extend the capex cycle. After India's 5G peak, a second carrier supplied the next leg of tower demand; in Helios's markets Orange, Axian or Vodacom in the DRC could play that role.
  2. Additions above about 3,500 in FY2027. Morgan Stanley already forecasts 3,400.
  3. A catch-up of 5 to 10 in H1 2027 EBITDA, if fuel costs under-recovered in 2026 are recovered. This catch-up is the earlier Analyst's conjecture.
  4. Collection of disputed revenue. Helios has left 50.4 of billed services unrecognised because collection is in doubt, and no broker models its recovery.
  5. Renewals appearing in the contracted-revenue schedule.

What would change my view. Airtel's capex guidance in May 2027 is the single most informative item, because it is the first hard evidence on operators' spending in 2028.

Against the market. Brokers' target prices rose 4% in the last month, and their notes still speak of upside risk. I expect brokers' numbers to end the next six months about where they began.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely to open on 18 March with a midpoint about 2.5% below consensus (75%) and then be raised in July and November (55-60%) only up to consensus, so the raise against 9-14% growth is about 0.2 and against consensus nil; consensus FY2027 EBITDA likely holds, FY2028 is more likely cut than raised (50% against 15%), and the narrative's next items (falling additions, a likely FY2026 EPS miss, capex above consensus, a convertible, the DRC law) lean negative. The figures' (5)% three-month EPS revision (16th percentile) fits a slightly unfavourable gap, coherent with the group's 45; the positive options (Airtel's May guide, disputed revenue of 50.4) keep it just below Carlsberg's mixed picture rather than at IMCD's.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price and peers

Bottom lineMomentum in guidance, estimates and the share price is strong and far better than at Helios's peers, but the momentum is mature and exposed to the weak optics of the first half of 2027.

Evidence: Helios leads its peers on every momentum measure.

  • Guidance. Helios raised guidance at three events in 2026 and added a FY2027 volume figure at the fourth.
  • Estimates. Consensus FY2027 EPS is up 10% over one month and 12% over twelve months; consensus FY2027 EBITDA is up 2% and 8% over the same periods. Target prices run from 290p to 315p at the three brokers whose research I have.
  • Price. The shares are 17.3% above a 200-day moving average that has risen in each of the last twelve months, they rank in the 84th percentile of the universe for relative strength, and they are close to their 52-week high of 247.6p.
  • Co-movement with peers. Over the latest six months, the European tower companies explain only 13% of the daily variance in Helios's share price.
  • Theme. The dashboard's thematic rating for the sector is D, and the portfolio's sector row is Underweight while US yields stay high.

Inference. Helios's momentum is strong on every company-specific measure and unique in its sector. Three details temper it.

  1. EPS revisions are five times the EBITDA revisions. The gap shows that the EPS revisions are the geared residual below EBITDA moving, not a stronger business.
  2. Flows have moved the stock more than estimates have. The six-month price return is only +0.9%, because the shares fell 23% from June to August 2026 on a founder's selling while guidance was being raised.
  3. A Buy share of 100% across five brokers can only fall.

So what. Momentum supports holding the shares through delivery. However, the most visible series, tenancy additions, will carry the narrative in 2027, and additions fall year on year for three quarters in the base case. New Street's target price, at about 242p, is already at the share price, and the chance of a first rating below Buy is about 35%.

Counter-case. Helios's decoupling from the sector could reverse. In past periods of stress, about half of the sector's share-price move passed through to Helios, so a shock to interest rates would hurt the shares despite the company's own delivery.

What would change my view. A first downgrade, or the share price falling through its 200-day average on a guidance or volume release that was in line with the base case, would mark perception overtaking fundamentals. I would read either event as an opportunity to buy.

Against the market. I agree with the market that momentum is strong. I differ on whether that momentum will last through the first half of 2027.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. Both measures are positive, so B; guidance was raised at three events in 2026, every broker rates Buy, the price is 17% above a 200-day average that has risen for twelve months and near its high, and momentum is far better than peers (revision score 10 against negative peers). I place it in the lower half of the band because the sell-side score is only just above neutral, the figures' three-month EPS revision is (5)% (16th percentile), the six-month price return is only +0.9% and the 100% Buy share can only fall.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Bottom lineThe forecasts are simple, trackable and low-risk at the level of EBITDA and cash, and of average risk at the level of EPS and the share price. The DRC is where a sudden, material and poorly understood risk sits.

Simplicity. The case is simple. One driver, tenancies, correlates 0.96 with EBITDA. The chain from operators' capex to Helios's EBITDA is short, and listed counterparties publish its links every quarter, so the driver can be checked about every six weeks.

Fragilities. The same simplicity means concentration: two customers provide 51% of revenue, and two countries provide about two-thirds of EBITDA. EPS is a residual after items that the company does not guide. And the business has never been tested, as an organic company, through a fall in operators' spending.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic. All EPS figures are on the model basis. From the model summary I derive EPS to three decimals of about 0.189, 0.225 and 0.261 for FY2027 to FY2029, and share counts of about 1,011m, 979m and 937m.

Judgement 1: volume. Additions are 500 a year lower in FY2027 and FY2028 (2,600 and 1,900).

  1. Management's rule of thumb: 500 tenancies are worth about 5 of EBITDA in their first year and 10 a year after.
  2. FY2027 EBITDA: 605.6 less 5 is about 601 (0.8)%.
  3. FY2028 EBITDA: less 10 for the 2027 shortfall and 5 for the 2028 shortfall gives 642 (2.3)%. FY2029 EBITDA: less 20 gives about 680 (2.9)%.
  4. FY2029 net income at a 27.5% tax rate: 244.9 less 14.5 is 230.4. EPS: 230.4 over 937m shares is 0.246, down 5.9%.
  5. Capex: 500 fewer additions, at 30% new towers (130,000 USD each) and 70% colocations (12,000 USD each), save about 24 a year.
  6. FY2027 equity free cash flow: 64.6, less 5 of EBITDA, plus 1.4 of tax saved, plus 24 of capex saved, is about 85, up 31%.

The mirror image holds for 500 more additions. A deeper miss, additions of 1,500 a year from FY2028, takes about 25 from FY2029 EBITDA and about 7% from FY2029 EPS.

Judgement 2: the DRC base stays whole.

(a) Renewal terms. The base case already gives up 12 of revenue and EBITDA in FY2029 to renewals.

  1. A 15% rate cut on the roughly 250 of DRC revenue from Airtel and Orange is 37.5, which is 25.5 more than the base case.
  2. FY2029 EBITDA: 699.8 less 25.5 is 674.3 (3.6)%.
  3. FY2029 net income falls by 18.5, to 226.4. EPS: 0.242, down 7.5%.
  4. With no concession at all, FY2029 EPS is 3.6% higher than the base case.

(b) The ownership law. If Helios had to sell 30% of its DRC unit (my rough arithmetic, an upper bound):

  1. The DRC produces about 30% of group EBITDA, about 197 in FY2028.
  2. After about 50 of depreciation, and tax at the 35% statutory rate, the DRC unit's profit before group financing is about 96.
  3. A 30% minority shareholder would take about 29 of that profit, which is 13% of FY2028 net income of 220.4.
  4. Sale proceeds offset the loss. At 7x EBITDA, 30% of the DRC unit is worth about 410; used to repay debt at 7%, the proceeds save about 29 of interest a year, which makes the sale roughly neutral for EPS. At half that price, the net cost is about 6% to 7% of EPS.

The accounting effect of a forced sale could be smaller than this, because the DRC unit still has tax losses. I cannot put a probability on the law applying to Helios: a February 2026 decree names the mobile operators, Helios holds a passive-infrastructure licence rather than an operator's licence, and Nigeria's regulator has shown that tower companies can be caught by rules written for operators.

Judgement 3: capital intensity. New towers stay at 40% of additions in FY2027 and FY2028 (base case: 35% and 30%).

  1. FY2027: 155 more new towers, each costing 118,000 USD more than a colocation, add 18 of capex. Equity free cash flow falls from 64.6 to about 46 (28)%.
  2. FY2028: 240 more new towers add 28 of capex. Equity free cash flow falls from 160.9 to about 133 (18)%.
  3. EPS: about 3 of extra depreciation and lease cost, about (1)%.
  4. Tenancy ratio at end-2028: 2.29x, where the base case has 2.34x.

Judgement 4: the bridge from EBITDA to EPS.

  1. Tax: 4 points on FY2027 pre-tax profit of 263.6 is 10.5, about 1 point of revenue. FY2027 EPS moves 5.5%.
  2. Currency: a loss of 30 on intercompany loans takes reported net income from 191.1 to 161.1 and reported EPS down 16%. Adjusted EPS and cash are unchanged. A currency loss of 20 or more in a year is about an even chance; the FY2023 loss was 86.

Judgement 5: the multiple.

  1. One turn of EV/EBITDA on FY2027 EBITDA is about 606 of value.
  2. Against a market value of about 3,200 to 3,500, one turn is 17% to 19% of the share price.
  3. A trough multiple of 6.5x to 7.0x FY2027 EBITDA, against 8.4x now, would mean a share-price fall of 25% to 35% if it happened today.

Sector precedents: Helios has retired one of the five classic tower risks and reduced another. Tower stocks have underperformed for five reasons:

Cause of past underperformancePrecedentHelios's exposure today
Rising interest ratesCellnex halvedExposed, through the multiple
Currency collapse where billing was localIHS in NigeriaLow: about 70% of EBITDA is in hard or pegged currencies
Customer distressAmerican Tower in IndiaExposed, through four large customers
Disputes over master lease agreementsInwit de-rated from about 16x to 11x EBITDAExposed, through four large customers
Debt-funded acquisitionsHelios itself fell 45% in 2023 at 5.1x leverageRetired

After a capex peak, the lull in operators' spending lasted two to three years in India and in the United States.

Trackability: most of the EPS uncertainty closes on one date. Second-half tax and currency, the settlement of the convertible bond and capex guidance all arrive with the results on 18 March 2027.

Inference and so what. The risks to the business and the risks to the shares differ in kind. Almost none of the listed risks reaches EBITDA or cash; most reach reported EPS or the multiple. The shares can therefore fall sharply on an event that leaves the forecasts intact, while the share price implied by a trough multiple rises 10% to 15% a year as EBITDA grows.

Counter-case. The business is less safe than its contracts suggest if the installed base becomes contestable. A material renewal concession, or the ownership law applying to towers, would make it contestable, and the record cannot show how likely either is, because Helios has never faced a fall in operators' spending as an organic business.

What would change my view. Disputed revenue rising above 55, a cut to guidance, or the DRC law being applied to towers.

Against the market. Brokers present Helios as low-risk because its revenue is contracted. I agree for the business, but I rate the equity as average-risk, because EPS is a residual of unguided lines and the DRC law has not been researched.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple and trackable (one driver correlating 0.96 with EBITDA, read every six weeks, FY2027 EBITDA within about 3% four times in five), but the memo's FY2027 reported EPS range is about (40)% to +12% because tax, currency and share count are unguided, leverage is 3.4x (net debt/EBITDA at the 82nd percentile), two customers give 51% and two countries two-thirds of EBITDA, and the DRC ownership law and cash-repatriation risks are sudden and unestimable, with a 25-35% fall to trough multiples. Between the groups' 40 and 62, I place it just below IMCD (simple model, similar leverage and EM currency) and level with OMV Petrom's concentrated sovereign interventions.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Bottom lineThe stock is late in the reinforcing phase of its upgrade cycle, and the first real test of a slide into the stalling phase comes in late 2027.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places the stock in the Broadening phase, but the facts point one step later.

  • The sell-side fully owns the thesis. Every broker rates the shares Buy and tells the same story.
  • Upgrades continue but are shrinking. Consensus FY2027 EBITDA rose about 3% in the last six months, after about 5% in the six months before.
  • The shares have risen by more than half in a year.
  • Growth is peaking. The growth rate of the visible driver, tenancy additions, peaked in the first half of 2026, and EBITDA growth peaks in the first half of 2027.

Inference. I place the stock late in the reinforcing phase, where delivery confirms a thesis the market already holds. One qualification is constructive: the shareholder register may still be broadening even though the sell-side thesis is complete. The founders' overhang has cleared, daily liquidity is about USD 10m, no large American broker covers the stock, and the first dividend opens the shares to income investors.

So what. In a reinforcing phase, shareholders earn their return from delivery and time rather than from surprise. The risk is a slide into the stalling phase between November 2027 and March 2028, when FY2028 volume and guidance are likely to come in below what consensus assumes.

Counter-case. The stock could move back into the broadening phase if operators extend their capex cycle, or if cash per share starts to compound visibly as capex falls.

What would change my view. Airtel's capex guidance in May 2027 would show the first of those routes, an extended capex cycle; the FY2027 capex guide on 18 March 2027 would show the second, falling capex.

Against the market. The brokers describe a broadening story, but their own estimates describe a reinforcing one.

Score: 51, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's late Reinforcing over the computed Turning/Inflecting and the dashboard's Broadening: the sell-side owns the thesis (100% Buy), upgrades are shrinking (FY2027 EBITDA +3% after +5%), additions' growth peaked in H1 2026 and EBITDA growth peaks in H1 2027, with a slide to Stalling possible from November 2027. A still-broadening register (founder overhang cleared, a first dividend, no large US broker) lifts it a point above BP's late Reinforcing but below Greggs.

#11 The fair multiple

Bottom lineThe guideline fair multiple is 42.33x two-year-forward earnings. My view is that about 20x is the fair multiple for this stock in this phase, because the history behind the guideline is dominated by years when earnings were close to zero.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 42.33x two-year-forward earnings is the 80th percentile of the stock's own valuation history, the level the rule sets for a stock in the Broadening phase. It is 138% above the current multiple of 17.79x.

My view. The logic of the guideline is sound: a stock in strong delivery deserves the upper part of its historical range. For Helios, however, the historical range itself is distorted, and I do not think 42.33x measures what investors will pay.

Evidence

  • Most of the valuation history is noise. The history covers 72 months. For the first 30 months, to April 2023, forward earnings were close to zero and the multiple ran from about 25x to 179x. Those multiples record how small the earnings were, not what investors valued.
  • The same 80th-percentile rule, applied to the meaningful months only, gives about 20x. Over the 42 months from May 2023, the 80th percentile of the multiple is about 20x and the median is about 18x (my arithmetic from the valuation history). The multiple touched 22.5x at the two peaks of the 2026 delivery phase.
  • The cross-check on enterprise value fails. At 42.33x earnings, the shares would be valued at about 17x forward EBITDA. European tower companies average 14.8x, Helios trades at 8.4x, and MTN is paying about 6x for IHS, the one large African tower transaction.
  • The economics support 8x to 10x EBITDA. New capital earns about 20% before tax against a cost of capital of about 11%, with EBITDA growth of 9% to 10% a year.

Inference. My fair multiple is about 20x two-year-forward earnings on the consensus basis, within a range of 18x to 22x. That multiple equals about 9.5x forward EBITDA and is 12% above today's multiple. It sits in the upper part of the range in which the stock has actually traded since it had earnings, which is what the guideline intends for a stock in delivery.

So what. The re-rating on offer is modest. Because the multiple is driven by the company rather than by the sector, Helios would have to earn any re-rating through three achievements: leverage reaching 3.0x with further credit-rating upgrades, renewals visibly continuing on existing terms, and a record of rising cash per share.

Counter-case for a higher multiple. A fall in US yields would lift the whole tower sector, and Helios at 18.6x current earnings stands beside Inwit at 19.7x while growing several times faster. In that setting a multiple of 22x to 25x is possible. I see no route to 42x that does not require earnings to disappoint, which would mechanically inflate the multiple.

What would change my view. A private transaction for African towers well above 6x EBITDA would raise my range; a material renewal concession would lower it to about 15x.

Against the market. Brokers' target prices of 290p to 315p equal about 20x to 22x today's two-year-forward consensus EPS, so my fair multiple is in line with the brokers and far below the guideline.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C; I place it in the upper half because the peer reading is a hair from cheap and the memo's meaningful-history check (median about 18x, 80th percentile about 20x since earnings appeared) puts today's 17.8x at the median for a business still in delivery, with a fair multiple about 12% higher. I do not go higher because a late-Reinforcing stock with frontier risk does not deserve a premium to its history, and 8.4x EBITDA against 14.8x for European towers is a deserved discount.

#12 Total shareholder return

Bottom lineThe return of record is +256.1% to 31 December 2027 and +338.5% to 30 June 2029, at the guideline multiple. The part of the return driven by earnings and dividends, about 18% a year, is the part I regard as dependable.

The return of record. The Financial Analyst's model gives the following returns at the guideline fair multiple.

Horizon, endingTotal shareholder returnAnnualisedValue per shareFrom dividendsFrom the multipleFrom earnings
The 18-month column, 31 December 2027+256.1%+216.8%8.43 GBP+1.4%+184.8%+24.6%
The three-year column, 30 June 2029+338.5%+76.6%10.37 GBP+2.4%+184.8%+53.1%

The multiple part and the earnings part multiply, and the dividend part adds: 1.246 times 2.848, less 1, plus 1.4%, gives +256%.

What drives each part of the return

  • Earnings (+24.6% and +53.1%): the dependable part. The earnings part is the growth in two-year-forward EPS, from about 0.21 today to 0.26 at the first horizon. By my approximate arithmetic, about 11 of the 24.6 points come from EBITDA growth, about 7 from fixed finance costs gearing that growth, and 5 to 6 from the falling share count. The drivers of the earnings part are judgements 1 to 4 in #9.
  • Dividends (+1.4% and +2.4%). The dividend part is small, because Helios returns cash mainly through buybacks, whose effect sits in the earnings part.
  • The multiple (+184.8%). The multiple part is the move from 14.9x today, on the model's EPS, to 42.33x. Without that move the 18-month return would be +26%, and the move rests entirely on the guideline.

Three cautions in reading the return of record

  1. The multiple part mixes two bases of EPS. The guideline multiple was measured on consensus EPS, where it is 138% above today's multiple. The model applies it to the model's own, higher EPS, where it is 184.8% above today's multiple. On a like-for-like basis, the return at the guideline multiple would be nearer +200%. This is my inference, and the Financial Analyst should confirm it.
  2. The first horizon rolls earnings forward 18 months in only about 13. The model's columns start from the last reported period, June 2026, while the share price is November's. The mismatch flatters the annualised figure. Over a true 18 months, the earnings part is worth about 17% to 19% a year.
  3. The three-year column runs past the last forecast year. Its two-year-forward earnings extend into 2031.

Inference. The return I would rely on is the unchanged-multiple line: about 18% a year from earnings and dividends, with a re-rating to 20x worth a further 12% once. Time cushions the downside. A trough multiple at the end of 2027 would leave the shares between about flat (measured on earnings, as in the table) and about 20% lower (measured at 6.5x to 7.0x EBITDA), whereas the same trough multiple today would cost 25% to 35%.

So what. The skew of the return is favourable but ordinary: good compounding, a modest re-rating option, and a drawdown risk concentrated in the next six months, before the earnings have rolled forward.

Counter-case. The earnings part could be 6 to 8 points lower on a volume miss or a DRC miss (#9), and the share-count contribution to the earnings part rests on buybacks that are not yet committed.

What would change my view. A different rule for setting the fair multiple, or evidence that investors will pay European tower multiples for African towers.

Against the market. Brokers' target prices imply returns of 22% to 33% over twelve months, which is close to my unchanged-multiple figure and a small fraction of the return of record.

Score: 79, set by the Rater. I weigh the return of record differently: it rests on a 42.33x guideline that the memo shows is distorted by near-zero early earnings and mixes EPS bases, so the central case is about +25-30% led by earnings and buybacks, B, with the three-year check (+56% unchanged, about 18% a year) supportive. I place it a little below the 82 that 27% maps to because the lower tail is concentrated in the next six months (about (20)% on trough EV/EBITDA) and part of the earnings leg rests on uncommitted buybacks.

#13 Summary conclusion

The verdictHelios is a high-quality, simple and well-run business in a strong demand cycle, and its next 18 months of EBITDA are largely installed already. The investment case is delivery of what the market already expects, so the return comes from earnings compounding at a high-teens rate at an unchanged multiple.

The foundations are robust where the forecasts need them to be: contracts that renew by default, local dominance, and an execution record without an operating miss.

The upside is ordinary rather than skewed. Consensus has absorbed the conservatism in guidance, the narrative already holds every favourable dynamic, and the stock is late in its upgrade cycle. A modest re-rating is available if the story moves from volume growth to cash per share.

Three things could make the case better than it looks today. Operators could extend their capex cycle, and Airtel's guidance in May 2027 will show that first. The optical negatives of the first half of 2027 could offer a lower share price while EBITDA growth is at its peak. And the results on 18 March 2027 will close much of the EPS uncertainty at a stroke.

One thing could make the case worse, and it deserves research now: whether the DRC's 30% local-ownership law reaches tower companies. A telecoms lawyer in Kinshasa, or a direct question to the company, would settle most of the uncertainty.

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 71, set by the Rater. A strong structural demand tailwind (70) and a funded capital-allocation harvest (62) reach profits with high certainty through FY2027 and give EPS growth of about 20% a year (A), well above the typical company, because tenancies are installed and finance costs fixed. It sits in the 75 level's lower part because the forces are narrow, past their volume peak and shifting to capital-heavy builds, so revenue growth slows to 5-6% and much of the EPS growth is gearing on decelerating EBITDA rather than accelerating change.

Foundations' Robustness: 74, set by the Rater. Local dominance, long, indexed, non-cancellable contracts that have renewed by default, 99.99% uptime and a ten-year unbroken EBITDA record through sovereign default and conflict (quality 66, delivery 76) give unusually stable and predictable operating foundations, which per Richard's CVS Group example can carry ordinary reported returns into the 75 band. It stops just below it because four operators give 72% of revenue and are becoming competitors, the markets are frontier sovereigns, leverage is 3.4x and earnings are clean only down to EBITDA.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 78, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits Demand-driven EPS Upgrader closely: one demand driver, a contracted step-up in EBITDA already installed, capacity and delivery proven, and earnings power geared by fixed costs and interest; that consensus already holds the step-up does not count here. One element is loose in the business itself: the demand impulse has peaked and is turning to capital-heavy coverage builds, with the colocation loop on new towers unproven, which holds it below the 80s.

Case Riskiness: 50, set by the Rater. This is the levels' simple operating case whose equity outcome is less predictable than its operating lines: EBITDA and cash are narrow and trackable, but reported EPS spans about (40)% to +12%, leverage is 3.4x, concentration is in two customers and two countries, and the DRC law and repatriation risks are sudden and unestimable (topic 9 at 45). It sits a little above topic 9 because the multiple is mid-range rather than stretched and most EPS uncertainty closes on one date, 18 March 2027, but the DRC risk is a potential major problem, not a paper cut.

Reading notes

How to read the numbers
  • Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2. I changed no forecast input.
  • EBITDA is the company's Adjusted EBITDA, which is also the brokers' measure. Consensus is the FactSet median of five brokers at 17 November 2026.
  • EPS has two bases, and the two must not be compared. The model's EPS leaves out the amortisation of acquired intangibles, share-based pay and minority interests, so it sits well above consensus for the same profit (FY2027: 0.19 against 0.14). On the brokers' own basis, the earlier Analyst estimates our EPS at 0.106, 0.148, 0.183 and 0.217 for FY2026 to FY2029, within 3% of consensus from FY2027.
  • Latest company data are the Q3 2026 trading update of 5 November 2026. The last full profit and loss account is for H1 2026.
  • Probabilities are the research Analysts' estimates, which I adopt unless I say otherwise.
  • Terms. A tenancy is one operator's equipment on one tower. A colocation is a tenancy added to a tower that already exists. The tenancy ratio is tenancies per tower. Recurring free cash flow is the company's measure: cash after maintenance capex, leases, tax and interest, and before growth capex. The DRC is the Democratic Republic of Congo. IMPACT 2030 is Helios's set of targets to 2030.

Notes. Charts drawn for this page take their figures from the memo text. Default charts and tables are from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model, as noted under each. Consensus is shown by named financial year throughout.

Peer set. The fifth name in the default peer data, INDUS Holding AG (shown in the relative-strength chart in #8), is a German industrial holding company and not Indus Towers; I leave it out of the peer analysis.

Open notes to the Financial Analyst. Two points await the Financial Analyst's confirmation: the model's net debt (#6) and the like-for-like return at the guideline multiple (#12).

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
